# Learning the Dark

Stand outside on a moonless night, somewhere far from any city, and give yourself to waiting. For the first few minutes you will see almost nothing. Your pupils will swell in their slow mechanical way, the chemistry of your retinas will begin to brew, and one by one the stars will arrive — the bright ones first, then the fainter ones, then whole constellations you had no idea were there. After half an hour the sky will have thickened to a depth you did not know the sky possessed, and if the night is clear you will see the Milky Way, which is not a cloud and not a river but the combined light of hundreds of billions of stars, too many and too faint for the eye to pull apart. Most people alive today have never seen it. By one estimate, more than eighty percent of North Americans and a third of all human beings cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because there is too much light in the sky. We have spent the past century abolishing the night, and we are only now beginning to add up what it cost.

For most of human history, night was a foreign country that everyone visited every day. It had laws and customs of its own. Travel stopped; roads that were merely inconvenient by day became genuinely dangerous after dark. Villages pulled inward around firelight. City gates closed. In many places the hours of darkness were divided into watches, and a bell or a watchman's cry announced their passage, so that even the night was habitable — partitioned, patrolled, made familiar. But it remained a different jurisdiction. The dead were said to walk; dreams were taken seriously as traffic from elsewhere; and the phrases we still use — nightmare, midnight, the dead of night, the witching hour — are fossils of an older fear, and an older reverence.

In the 1990s, the historian Roger Ekirch began noticing something strange in the records of pre-industrial Europe. Again and again — in letters, diaries, court testimony, ballads, medical texts, in English and French and Italian — he came across references to a "first sleep." Not a metaphor: a period of sleep people entered a few hours after nightfall, slept deeply, and then rose from, deliberately, into a stretch of quiet wakefulness. During this interval — an hour, sometimes two — people prayed, reflected on their dreams, read by ember-light, talked softly, made love, or simply lay still in the dark. Then they went down again into a second sleep that lasted until dawn. Ekirch found the pattern across centuries and continents, so ordinary to the people living it that they rarely thought to explain it.

In 1992, a researcher named Thomas Wehr accidentally reproduced it. He had taken volunteers and shut them in laboratories with fourteen hours of darkness every night — an approximation of a winter's light, far closer to what our ancestors lived with than our own eight lit hours ever are. At first the subjects simply slept long. But after a few weeks their sleep quietly split in two: a solid stretch, then a calm hour or so of wakefulness in the middle of the night — not anxious, not restless, but serene, something like meditation, with its own measurable chemistry — followed by a second sleep. Given darkness, the old night reassembled itself, as though it had been waiting in us all along.

Darkness governed so much of life because light was ruinously expensive. A tallow candle — dim, smoky, smelling of burnt fat — could cost a working man the better part of an hour's wage, which meant that burning a candle was burning money, literally, and people did it sparingly. The poor burned rushlights, reeds dipped in grease, each one good for only minutes of illumination, and counted them like coins. Whale fleets crossed the oceans in pursuit of spermaceti, the waxy oil in the sperm whale's head, because it made candles that burned clean and bright; an entire global industry rose and fell on the human hunger for a few more visible hours of evening. Moonlight was a public utility. Farmers planned work around it. To burn the midnight oil was not a figure of speech but a line in a household budget.

And yet the old dark was not only a place of fear and scarcity. It had its freedoms. The day belonged to masters, markets, and obligations; the night, in many places, belonged to everyone else. After the household slept, servants and neighbors and lovers found hours the day never offered. Around fires, stories were told — and it is no accident that the ghost story, the folk tale, the long comic saga grew up in darkness, told by people with nothing to do with the dark hours and nothing to look at but one another. Night had its own economy too: smugglers, poachers, runaways, and thieves all worked the night shift of history. The dark concentrated community the way the day dispersed it. Fear and intimacy were braided together in it, as perhaps they always are.

Then we conquered it. Gasworks arrived first: London's Pall Mall was lit by gas in 1807, and within decades the lamplighter, going his rounds at dusk with pole and taper, was a fixture of every great city. Kerosene came, cheaper than whale oil, and quietly did more for whales than any law had. Then, in 1882, Edison's Pearl Street Station began sending electricity through Lower Manhattan, and the economics of the night inverted. For the first time in the species' history, darkness became more expensive than light. Factories learned to run around the clock. Cities stopped going out. What had been a foreign country was annexed, mapped, and settled, and within a few generations most of humanity was only passing through it — asleep, with a lamp on.

Now the night is lit from within by everything — streetlights and billboards and stadium glare, and inside it all a smaller light in every hand. In 1994, when an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles, residents reportedly called observatories and emergency services to ask about a vast, strange, silvery cloud that had appeared over the suddenly darkened city. It was the Milky Way. People were seeing, with alarm, the galaxy they lived inside. Some of the callers had lived their entire lives beneath it and had never once seen it.

Something is lost in that. The stars are humanity's oldest library. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open ocean holding star-paths in their heads, reading latitude off the sky. Farmers watched the Pleiades rise to know when to plant and when to expect rain. Whole moral and seasonal cosmologies were stored overhead, in patterns anyone could read, free, for the price of walking outside and looking up. Most of that library is functionally closed now — not burned, just shelved behind a glare most of us cannot see past. A child can memorize the constellations from a book and never once have seen one.

But the human loss is only part of it, and maybe the smaller part, because night is not merely scenery for our own lives. It is infrastructure for everyone else's. Sea turtle hatchlings, emerging from their nests on the sand, do what their kind has always done: they crawl toward the brighter horizon, which for millions of years has meant the moonlit sea.
